newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bof council member sees room for French rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Bof council member sees room for French rate cut.

text.p: Paul Marchelli, a member of the Bank of France's monetary policy council, said on Wednesday he saw scope for a cut of as much as 50 basis points in the central bank's 3.20 percent intervention rate over coming months.
In an interview with Reuters, Marchelli said he was speaking in a personal capacity and Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet was responsible for giving the official position.

"We are at 3.20, but I think that in the months to come, if we were to cut by ... perhaps 20, 30 or even 50 basis points, it would not be ridiculous given current market sentiment and our (economic) fundamentals," he said.
The Bank of France last cut its intervention rate, which sets the floor on money market rates, to 3.20 percent from 3.25 percent on October 31.
Marchelli said any cut in rates should be geared towards stimulating faster economic growth and tackling unemployment, which he described as his primary concern.
"Right now it is important that cutting interest rates contributes to an increase in growth," he said.
He said he was not, however, saying there should be a devaluation of the franc.
"I do not see why it should be necessary to think about a franc devaluation," he said.

The franc's current pivot rate of 3.35 against the mark in the European Monetary System "corresponds with French reality," he said. A devaluation would be both clumsy and fail to reflect the real French economy.

Former French president Valery Giscard d'Estaing stirred up a debate about the level of the franc last month when he suggested France should let its currency depreciate sharply to boost growth and create jobs.
The public debate prompted France and Germany to reaffirm their commitment to the existing franc/mark level.
Marchelli said any interest rate moves would have to be weighed carefully, but the French economy should be able to bear a cut even if the closely watched Bundesbank did not make one.

"Is it possible to cut rates further? My personal response is yes. Not any old how, or in any conditions, but also bearing in mind that our rate policy can take some distance from the Bundesbank's rates," he said.

"What I mean by that is that French economic fundamentals...should allow us, even if Buba does not move, to cut rates because we still have a useful margin which will undoubtedly be significant for the economy."
Marchelli said French monetary policy had been successful in providing the best possible interest rates for the economy.
